Why Goryu?
GitHub
🎯

Agents get it right the first time

A small, regular API constrains codegen — fewer ways to call it means fewer ways to get it wrong. Go's compiler rejects the rest on the spot. If an LLM can't reliably write correct Goryu, the API is too clever — so it isn't.

🔒

Secure by default

Security headers, CSRF, JWT & sessions with unified invalidation, OAuth2/OIDC, passkeys, RBAC, and an audit log — on every response path. The agent physically can't skip the security basics.

🔋

Batteries included, few dependencies

Router, DB, validation, monitoring, health checks, graceful shutdown — wired from day one. Fewer libraries means fewer versions and APIs for an agent to hallucinate. One binary, zero assembly.

🔍

No magic — readable enough to trust

Explicit, readable Go. No reflection soup, no hidden control flow. You — or a non-technical reviewer — can read what the agent shipped and believe it's safe to deploy.

🤖

AI-native

SSE & typed streaming, Bind[T] + JSON Schema, token/cost metering, prompt caching, provider proxying, and eval recording. Build LLM backends without hand-rolling the plumbing.

⚡

As fast as Gin

Radix-tree router and optimized middleware chains — Gin-class throughput with 10× more built in. The simple REST case never pays for features it doesn't use.

Describe it. Your agent builds it. It compiles — and it's safe to ship. ​

You don't hand-write boilerplate anymore — you direct an agent. So the framework's job changed: it's no longer just pleasant to type, it has to be the thing your agent generates correctly and that you can read well enough to trust.

Goryu is built for exactly that. The API is small and regular, so a coding agent has few wrong turns to take. It's Go, so the compiler catches the rest before you ever run it. And it's secure by default, so the one thing agents reliably get wrong — the security basics — is handled whether the agent thinks about it or not.

go
package main

import "github.com/arthurlch/goryu"

func main() {
    app := goryu.New(goryu.Config{AppName: "api"})

    app.GET("/health", func(c *goryu.Ctx) {
        _ = c.JSON(200, goryu.Map{"status": "ok"})
    })

    app.POST("/users", func(c *goryu.Ctx) {
        user, err := goryu.Bind[CreateUser](c) // parse + validate
        if err != nil {
            _ = c.JSON(400, goryu.Map{"error": err.Error()})
            return
        }
        _ = c.JSON(201, user)
    })

    app.Run(":3000")
}

type CreateUser struct {
    Email string `json:"email" jsonschema:"format=email"`
    Name  string `json:"name"  jsonschema:"minLength=1"`
}

func (u CreateUser) Validate() error { /* ... */ return nil }
go
package main

import (
    "github.com/arthurlch/goryu"
    "github.com/arthurlch/goryu/middleware/aimeter"
)

type Token struct {
    Content string `json:"content"`
    Done    bool   `json:"done,omitempty"`
}

func main() {
    app := goryu.New(goryu.Config{AppName: "chat"})

    // Token/cost metering + per-key limits, out of the box.
    app.Use(aimeter.New(aimeter.Config{
        PromptCostPer1K:     0.003,
        CompletionCostPer1K: 0.015,
    }))

    app.POST("/chat/stream", func(c *goryu.Ctx) {
        // Stream typed tokens over SSE.
        _ = goryu.SSEJSON(c, "token", func(send func(Token) error) error {
            for tok := range generate(c) {
                if err := send(Token{Content: tok}); err != nil {
                    return err
                }
            }
            return send(Token{Done: true})
        })
    })

    app.Run(":3000")
}
go
package main

import (
    "os"

    "github.com/arthurlch/goryu"
    "github.com/arthurlch/goryu/aiproxy"
    "github.com/arthurlch/goryu/middleware/promptcache"
)

func main() {
    app := goryu.New()

    // Cache identical prompts (POST-aware, streaming-safe).
    app.Use(promptcache.New())

    px := aiproxy.New(aiproxy.Config{
        BaseURL: "https://api.openai.com",
        APIKey:  os.Getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
    })

    // Stream straight through to the provider (SSE passthrough).
    app.POST("/v1/chat/completions", func(c *goryu.Ctx) {
        _ = px.Stream(c, "/v1/chat/completions")
    })

    app.Run(":3000")
}

Why this matters now ​

Agents freeballing raw net/http produce a different shape every time, with different security gaps, and nobody can review fifty bespoke services by hand. Goryu makes agent output uniform, safe, and auditable — so the person directing the agent can actually ship it.

🎯 Right the first time ​

A regular, predictable API constrains what an agent can generate, so it generates correct Goryu. The compiler catches the rest before you run it.

Meet the CLI →

A CLI that does the boring parts — and feeds your agent ​

Goryu ships a real CLI — scaffold a project, generate handlers/models/middleware, run a hot-reloading dev server, inspect your routes, and expose your project to AI agents over MCP. It generates idiomatic Goryu code, so a human and a coding agent produce the same clean, reviewable output.

bash
# Scaffold a project and start building
goryu init myapp --template=api
goryu generate handler users --type=crud
goryu scaffold ai assistant --kind=rag     # a RAG endpoint, fully wired

# Develop, inspect, ship
goryu dev --port 8080                       # hot-reloading dev server
goryu routes list                           # inspect the route table
goryu build --static                        # production binary

# Let AI agents drive your project
goryu mcp                                    # MCP server (list routes, scaffold, run)

Principles ​

  1. If an LLM can't reliably generate correct Goryu code, the API is too clever. The regular, predictable API is a feature for people and agents alike.
  2. Built to be directed, not just typed. The same clean API serves the human reviewing and the agent writing.
  3. No magic. Read the source and understand it — because trusting what ships now matters more than typing it.
  4. Secure by default, on every response path. Not an afterthought, not opt-in.
  5. The simple case stays simple. A hand-written REST API never pays for AI features it doesn't use.
  6. The core stays small and stable; breadth lives in contrib.
